summary: States the problem and lists requirements for a GEOPRIV Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol. Such a protocol would let a device ask a Location Information Server for its location, either as actual coordinates or as a reference. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Your device sometimes does not know where it is, but a helper in the network might. This document lists what a protocol for asking that helper must be able to do.

subtitle: What a protocol for asking the local network 'where am I?' has to do, and why the problem is harder than it sounds.

tldr.problem: A device often does not know where it is, but the access network it connects through often does. There is no agreed way for the device to ask the network for its location.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the scenarios, the ways a Location Information Server (LIS) could be discovered, the identifiers a LIS could use to look up a device, and ten requirements (L7-1 to L7-10) for a GEOPRIV Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement, not a protocol. The discovery and identifier sections explicitly record options without consensus.

facts.label: Two purposes
facts.value: Location by Value and Location by Reference

facts.label: Discovery options
facts.value: DHCP, DNS, redirect rule, multicast query, anycast

today: RFC 5687 is Informational and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a statement of the problem and requirements, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: The Problem and the Two Goals
sections.content:
RFC 5687 is a problem statement for a GEOPRIV Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol (L7 LCP). The protocol runs between a device and a Location Information Server (LIS), a node in the access network that can determine the device's location.

The protocol has two purposes. The first is Location by Value (LbyV): the device obtains its own location. The second is Location by Reference (LbyR): the device obtains a reference, such as a SIP presence-based URI or an HTTP/HTTPS URI, that others can use to get the location. The requirements for LbyR are in a separate document.

The RFC does not describe how the access network provider works out where the device is. That depends on link-layer technologies and deployment environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine asking the school office, 'Which room am I in?' The answer can be the room itself, or a note that says 'ask the office later'. This document is about how to ask the office.

sections.title: Network Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three environments: a fixed-wired DSL network, a mobile (moving) network, and a wireless hotspot. It also names airport, campus and 3G networks and enterprise networks as targets.

In the fixed-wired case the customer premises often has a home router that runs a NAPT and a DHCP server, plus Network Termination Equipment (NTE). The RFC notes that the NTE is a legacy device that in many cases cannot be modified to deliver location to the host, and the same is true of the NAPT and DHCP device.

In the moving-network case, such as a fixed-wireless antenna, buses, trains or airplanes, end devices may be completely unaware that they are moving. In the hotspot case, a moving host gets location or a reference from the LIS through an access point.
sections.plainLanguage: The device might be behind a home router that cannot be changed, or on a train that moves without the laptop noticing. A good protocol has to work in all these places.

sections.title: Discovering the LIS
sections.content:
Before a device can ask for its location, it must find the LIS. The RFC assumes the LIS is in the local subnet or the access network and lists the options discussed by the design team. It states plainly that these are included to show challenges and that there is no consensus on any of them.

  • DHCP-based discovery: can deliver the FQDN or IP address of the LIS, but may not work with legacy devices such as the NTE in the fixed-wired scenario.
  • DNS-based discovery: learn the access network's domain name (for example from a STUN-learned public address and a reverse lookup), then fetch the DNS SRV or NAPTR record.
  • Redirect rule: an access network entity redirects packets sent to a registered port to the LIS, as captive portals do for HTTP. This needs deep packet inspection.
  • Multicast query: works only on the local link.
  • Anycast: an anycast address routes discovery packets to the nearest LIS.

Whatever is used, the access network must prevent man-in-the-middle adversaries from posing as a LIS, and the device must be able to confirm the LIS is authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: First you need to find the office. You could be handed the address, look it up in a phone book, shout and hope the right person hears, or head to the nearest office. Each way has problems, and you must also make sure it is the real office.

sections.title: Identifiers for Location Lookup
sections.content:
The LIS needs some identifier to look up where a device is. A good identifier must be learnable by the device, usable by the LIS for location determination, and secure: an off-path adversary MUST NOT be able to obtain another device's location, and an on-path adversary in the same subnet SHOULD NOT be able to spoof another device's identifier.

The RFC reviews candidates, again without recommending one:

  • MAC address: not carried beyond one IP hop, so usually unavailable to the LIS.
  • ATM VPI/VCI: generally seen only by the DSL modem.
  • Ethernet switch and port number: available only in certain networks, such as enterprises.
  • Cell ID: in cellular data networks, and possibly not visible to the device.
  • Host Identity Protocol identifier and Cryptographically Generated Address (IPv6 only).
  • Network Access Identifier and the Broadband Forum unique client identifier.
  • IP address: behind a NAT the LIS sees only the NAT's public address. It allows a return routability check, but on a shared medium such as hotel WLAN an eavesdropper could spoof an address and learn, for example, room numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: To find you, the office needs a name tag. Some tags are hidden from the office, some can be copied by a sneaky person, and some only work in certain buildings.

sections.title: The Ten Requirements
sections.content:
Section 6 lists requirements L7-1 to L7-10 for the L7 LCP:

  • L7-1: carry different identifiers, or define a mandatory-to-implement one from the realm the location service maps.
  • L7-2: support a broad range of mobility, from devices that move only between reboots to devices that move continuously.
  • L7-3: not assume a business or trust relationship between the Application Service Provider and the Access Network Provider.
  • L7-4: assume a trust and business relationship between the L2 and L3 provider.
  • L7-5: consider legacy devices such as residential NATs and NTEs that cannot be upgraded.
  • L7-6: assume at least one end of a VPN is aware of the VPN.
  • L7-7: not assume prior network access authentication.
  • L7-8: not assume devices know the access network topology.
  • L7-9: define a mandatory-to-implement LIS discovery mechanism.
  • L7-10: when a LIS creates a PIDF-LO, put the <geopriv> element into the <device> element.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say the protocol must work with old equipment, moving devices and strangers, must have a standard way to find the office, and must package the answer in a standard envelope.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Using such a protocol exposes the device, and its user, to the privacy risk that an unauthorized entity receives location information. Getting confidential location to the requestor depends on four steps: the client MUST be able to discover a LIS, the client MUST authenticate the discovered LIS, the LIS MUST be able to determine location and return it to the authorized entity, and the LIS MUST exchange messages securely without eavesdropping or tampering.

The RFC says security requirements appear throughout the document and points to the GEOPRIV architecture work for the broader discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Where you are is private. You must find the real office, not an impostor, and nobody should be able to listen in on the answer.

items.title: DHCP
items.text: Delivers the LIS name or address, but legacy devices may block it.

items.title: DNS
items.text: Learn the access network domain, then fetch SRV or NAPTR records.

items.title: Redirect rule
items.text: Packets to a registered port are redirected to the LIS.

items.title: Multicast query
items.text: Works only on the local link.

items.title: Anycast
items.text: Discovery packets reach the nearest LIS.
